summary: This unit teaches you to produce clear, correct engineering drawings of simple fabricated parts. You will learn to use drawing equipment, set out a sheet with a border and title block, use the standard types of line, draw views in first-angle and third-angle projection, choose a scale, dimension a part so that it cannot be misread, make isometric and oblique drawings, draw sectional views and assembly drawings, and check a drawing before it is issued. You will also see how CAD compares with drawing by hand.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423). An **engineering drawing** gives exact information about a part: its shape, its sizes, the material and how it is to be made. In this unit you learn to **prepare** such drawings yourself, by hand with drawing instruments, to the agreed rules that let any welder, machinist or inspector read them the same way.

Fabricators draw all the time: a detail drawing of a bracket before it is cut, a sketch for a customer, an assembly drawing of a gate or a stand with its parts list, or a record drawing of a part that must be made again. A clear drawing saves material, time and arguments; a careless one causes parts that do not fit.
**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 2 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres. You need a steady hand, a sharp pencil and patience; you do not need to be an artist.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Study the part or sketch, choose the front view and the number of views, the projection method, the scale and the sheet size.
Use and care for drawing equipment
Fix the paper squarely and use the T-square, set squares, compass, dividers, protractor, scale rule and pencils correctly, keeping the work clean.
Draw the border and the title block, and space the views evenly with room for dimensions.
Use the correct lines and lettering
Thick outlines, dashed hidden detail, chain centre lines, thin dimension lines, cutting planes and break lines; neat capital letters.
Draw lined-up views in first-angle or third-angle projection, projecting sizes from view to view, and show the projection symbol.
Choose a standard scale, work out drawn sizes, and always write the real sizes.
Give every size needed once, clearly, outside the views, from datums where it matters, with Ø, R, notes and tolerances.
Draw isometric and oblique views, including circles as ellipses.
Show inside detail with a sectional view, and show how parts fit together with an assembly drawing and parts list.
Check every view, size and note; record revisions; store drawings flat and dry; ask when information is missing.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on equipment, lines, projection, dimensioning, scales, pictorial drawing, sections, the title block and checking.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms and abbreviations such as CAD, PCD, R, THK and 1:1, and simple sizes) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: detail drawings of the parts of a small welded bracket in orthographic projection, with an assembly drawing and parts list; and an isometric drawing and a sectional view of a fabricated part. The assessor checks the layout, the line types, the projection, the dimensions and the title block, and how you check other people's drawings.

blocks.note: Most marks are lost on small things: a missing projection symbol, a size given twice, a dimension written as the drawn size instead of the real size, or a title block left half empty. Check these every time.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A drawing is how a designer tells the people who make, inspect and buy a part exactly what is wanted. Many people read the same drawing: the designer, the person who orders the material, the fabricator and welder, the machinist, the inspector and sometimes the customer. They may never meet, so the drawing must mean the same thing to all of them.

That is why drawings follow **agreed rules (standards)** for lines, views, symbols and dimensions. Most training centres in the Caribbean teach the British and international (ISO) rules; drawings from the United States follow American rules, which differ in some details, such as the projection method. The ideas are the same.

head: Type
What it shows
Example
rows: A quick drawing by hand, without instruments, to show an idea or record sizes; marked NTS (not to scale)
Sizes of a broken bracket taken on site
One part, with every view, size, note and the material needed to make it
A base plate with its holes
How the parts fit together, with item numbers, a parts list and the main sizes
A water-tank stand with its legs, frame and braces
A small area drawn again at a larger scale so that it can be seen clearly
A notch or a small chamfer shown at 2:1
A 3D-looking view (isometric or oblique) that is easy to picture
A sketch of a bracket for a customer

blocks.h: When the rules are not followed

ul: A hidden edge drawn as a thick line is read as a visible edge.
A drawing with no projection symbol is read the wrong way round, so a hole ends up on the wrong side.
A size given twice with two different values leaves the fabricator guessing.
A missing size is guessed or measured off the paper.
The results are parts made wrongly, wasted material and time, parts that do not fit, unsafe products and arguments about who is to blame.

blocks.h: Drawing by hand and with CAD

blocks.p: **CAD** stands for computer-aided design (or computer-aided drafting): drawing with a computer program. Many workshops use both: a hand sketch to plan, and CAD for the final drawing.

head: Point
Drawing by hand
Drawing with CAD
rows: Simple, cheap instruments; no electricity needed
A computer, software, a printer and training, which all cost money; needs power
Quick for a simple sketch or a one-off part; slow for complex drawings
Slower to start; much quicker for complex work and repeats
Quick to change; parts and whole drawings can be copied and reused
Depends on the skill of the person drawing
Very accurate; lines and text are the same every time
Photocopies; paper must be stored flat and dry
Printed at any scale, emailed, stored and backed up as files
Builds a good understanding of projection
Some programs make 3D models and send cutting paths to machines such as plasma cutters

blocks.note: Learning to draw by hand is still the best way to understand views, projection and dimensions. CAD does the drawing faster, but it will not tell you which views a part needs or whether your dimensions make sense.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Equipment and setting up the sheet

head: Item
How it is used
Care
rows: A flat, smooth surface with a straight working edge; the paper is fixed to it
Keep the surface clean and the edges undamaged
Slides against the edge of the board (the left edge if you are right-handed) to draw horizontal lines
Keep the blade straight and clean; do not use it as a hammer or ruler for cutting
Rest on the T-square to draw vertical lines and lines at 30°, 45° and 60°; used together they also give 15° and 75°
Keep the edges clean and unchipped
Draws circles and arcs, with a point on one leg and a lead on the other
Keep the lead sharp and level with the point; cover the point
Transfer sizes and step off equal distances
Keep the points sharp and covered
Measures at the chosen scale (for example 1:2 or 1:5) without working out every size
Never draw lines along it with a knife or use it as a straight edge for cutting
Hard pencils for light lines, softer ones for dark lines and lettering
The shield is a thin plate with slots; it lets you rub out one line without spoiling the lines next to it
Circle, ellipse and lettering templates for neat work quickly

head: Grade
Use
rows: Light, thin construction lines, and thin lines such as dimension and hatching lines
Lining in the thick outlines, and lettering
Sketching; too soft for instrument drawing, as it smudges

blocks.p: Pencils run from very hard (9H) through H, F and HB to very soft (9B). The harder the lead, the lighter and finer the line. Clutch (mechanical) pencils in 0.3 mm and 0.5 or 0.7 mm leads give an even thin or thick line without sharpening.
Each size is half of the one above it: cut an A3 sheet in half, halving its long side, and you have two A4 sheets.

flow: Line the bottom edge of the paper up with the T-square
Tape or clip the corners so that the paper cannot move
Draw the border lightly, a set distance in from the edges (often about 10 mm, or as the Centre's sheet shows), then line it in thick
Draw the title block, usually in the bottom right-hand corner
Work out the space each view needs, and mark the positions lightly
Draw the views with light construction lines first

blocks.p: The **title block** holds the information about the drawing. A typical one includes:

ul: The title (the name of the part) and the drawing number
The scale, and the projection symbol
The units: for example ALL DIMENSIONS IN MILLIMETRES
The material, and the quantity if needed
General tolerances, if the drawing has them
Drawn by, checked by, and the dates
The revision letter or number, and the sheet number
Use plain **capital letters**, upright and evenly spaced.
Notes and dimension figures are usually about 3.5 mm high; the title and drawing number larger, often 5–7 mm.
Draw two faint guide lines for each line of lettering so that the letters are all the same height.

blocks.h: Keeping the drawing clean and safe

ul: Wash your hands and wipe your instruments before you start.
Lift the T-square and set squares rather than sliding them over finished lines, and cover finished parts with a clean sheet of paper.
Brush away eraser crumbs with a brush or a clean cloth, not the side of your hand.
Store finished drawings **flat in a drawer or rolled in a tube**, kept dry. Never fold them small or leave them in the workshop.
Keep compass and divider points covered; sit upright; take short breaks to rest your eyes and back.

blocks.p: Each **type of line** has one meaning. Learn them exactly: the reader of your drawing relies on them.

head: Line
What it looks like
What it is used for
rows: Dimension lines, projection (extension) lines, leader lines, hatching, and short centre lines
Hidden outlines and edges, behind the surface you are looking at
Long dash, short dash (dot), long dash
Centre lines, lines of symmetry and pitch circles
Thin chain, thick at the ends and where it changes direction
A chain line with thick ends, arrows and letters
Cutting planes: where a section is taken and which way it is viewed
A light wavy line, or a straight line with zigzags
Break lines: where part of a view is broken off, or where a long part is shortened
Neighbouring parts shown for reference, and other positions of moving parts

blocks.p: Thick lines are about twice as thick as thin lines: for example about 0.7 mm and 0.35 mm, or 0.5 mm and 0.25 mm. What matters is that the difference is easy to see.

ul: Draw everything first with light construction lines, then line in. Light lines can be rubbed out or lined in later.
Centre lines cross at the long dashes, not at the gaps, and run a short way (a few millimetres) past the outline. Every hole and round part has its centre lines.
Hidden lines start and finish with a dash touching the outline.
Where two lines fall in the same place, a visible line wins over a hidden line, and a hidden line wins over a centre line.
Keep every line of one type the same darkness and thickness over the whole sheet.

head: Symbol or abbreviation
Meaning
Example
rows: Across flats (of a nut or hexagon)
4 × Ø10 means four holes, each 10 mm in diameter

blocks.note: Write abbreviations in capitals, as shown, and do not invent your own. If a drawing must use an unusual abbreviation, write it out in a note.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Orthographic projection** shows an object in separate flat views, each one looking straight at one side. Each view shows two of the three sizes (length, height and depth) at their true size. Together, two or three lined-up views describe the whole shape.

blocks.h: Choosing the front view and the number of views

ul: Choose as the front view the side that **shows the most about the shape**, with the fewest hidden lines, usually with the part in its working position and its longest side across the sheet.

Draw as few views as will describe the part fully. A round bar with a hole across it needs two views. A flat plate may need only one view with a thickness note (for example 8 THK). A bracket usually needs three.

blocks.p: There are two ways of arranging the views. They use the same views; only their places on the sheet differ.

head: Point
First-angle projection
Third-angle projection
rows: Each view is placed on the far side of the front view from where it is seen
Each view is placed on the same side as it is seen from
To the right of the front view
To the left of the front view
To the left of the front view
To the right of the front view
British and European drawings, and many training centres in the Caribbean
Drawings from the United States and Canada

blocks.p: The method is shown by the **projection symbol** in the title block: a cone with its top cut off, drawn as a side view (a trapezium) and an end view (two circles). In the first-angle symbol the circles are drawn beside the **large** end of the trapezium; in the third-angle symbol they are beside the **small** end. Without the symbol, the reader cannot know where each view comes from.

blocks.note: Equipment and drawings from the United States use third-angle projection and inch sizes. Look for the symbol and the units before you read any view, and when you redraw a part, say clearly which method you have used.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: The views are **lined up** so that sizes can be projected from one view to another, instead of being measured again.
Heights are projected **across** from the front view to the end view.
Lengths are projected **down** (first angle) or **up** (third angle) from the front view to the plan.
Depths are carried from the plan to the end view through a **45° line** (the mitre line), or transferred with dividers.

flow: Study the part or sketch; choose the front view and the views needed
Choose the projection method and the scale; set out the border and title block
Work out the spacing of the views
Draw the centre lines and the main outline of the front view lightly
Project heights across to the end view and lengths to the plan; draw the 45° line and carry the depths
Add holes, slots and hidden edges in every view
Check the views against each other and against the part
Line in with the correct line types, then add dimensions, notes and the title block

blocks.p: Think of an angle bracket: a base leg 100 mm long with a Ø12 hole, and an upright leg 80 mm high with a Ø10 hole. In the front view, looking at the L shape from the side, neither hole can be seen, so both show as **thin dashed lines** running through the thickness of each leg, with a centre line. In the plan, the hole in the base shows as a circle, and in the end view the hole in the upright shows as a circle, both with centre lines. If a view would be crowded with hidden lines, a sectional view may show the inside more clearly.

blocks.note: Check that every edge appears in every view: as a visible line, a hidden line or a point. A line that appears in one view must line up with something in the views beside it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **scale** is the ratio of the size on the drawing to the real size of the part. It is written as **drawing size : real size**.

head: Kind
Standard scales
Meaning
Use
rows: The drawing is the same size as the part
At 1:5, 1 mm on the drawing stands for 5 mm on the part
Parts too big for the sheet: frames, gates, stands
At 2:1, the drawing is twice the real size

ul: Drawn size = real size ÷ the scale's second number (for reductions). At 1:5, a 600 mm part is drawn 600 ÷ 5 = 120 mm long.
For enlargements, multiply: at 2:1, a 15 mm part is drawn 30 mm long.
Real size = drawn size × the scale's second number. On a 1:20 drawing, a line 36 mm long stands for 36 × 20 = 720 mm.
A scale rule does the sum for you: read the 1:5 edge and it shows real sizes directly.

blocks.note: **Dimensions always show the real size**, whatever the scale. On a 1:5 drawing of a 600 mm bar, the dimension says 600, not 120. The part is made to the numbers written on the drawing.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Compare the size of the part, with all its views, the gaps between them and room for dimensions, with the space inside the border. Choose the **largest standard scale that fits**, so the drawing is clear but not crowded. Write the scale in the title block. A view drawn at a different scale, such as an enlarged detail, is marked with its own scale.

blocks.note: Never measure a size off a drawing (scaling the drawing) to make a part. Prints shrink and stretch, and the drawing may not be exactly to scale. If a size is missing, ask the person who drew it or your supervisor.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Engineering drawings are dimensioned in **millimetres**, and a note in the title block says so. When you redraw a part from an inch drawing, convert every size: **1 inch = 25.4 mm**. For example 0.5 in = 12.7 mm, 3/8 in ≈ 9.5 mm, and 6 in = 152.4 mm. Round sensibly, and check with your supervisor where a size must match an inch bolt or pipe.

blocks.h: Spacing the views on the sheet

blocks.p: Example: an A3 sheet (420 × 297 mm) with a 10 mm border leaves a space of 400 × 277 mm, and the title block takes about 40 mm at the bottom. The front view is 160 mm wide and 90 mm high, the end view 60 mm wide, and the plan 60 mm deep. Allow 30 mm between views for dimensions.

head: Direction
Sum
Spare space shared out
rows: 90 + 30 + 60 = 180 mm used; 277 − 40 = 237 mm available; 237 − 180 = 57 mm spare

blocks.p: Mark these positions lightly before you draw, so that the views are balanced, have room for dimensions and stay clear of the title block.
Dimensions tell the maker the sizes. They must be **complete, clear and given once**, so that the part can be made without measuring the drawing or guessing.

head: Part
How it is drawn
rows: Thin; starts a small gap (about 1 mm) from the outline, so it is not mistaken for part of it, and runs a little (about 2–3 mm) past the dimension line
Thin, with an arrowhead at each end touching the projection lines; at least about 8–10 mm from the outline and from the next dimension line
Neat, closed and filled in, about 3 mm long, all the same size
The size in millimetres, written clearly above the middle of the dimension line (or in a gap in it), readable from the bottom or the right-hand side of the sheet
A thin line from a note to the feature, ending in an arrowhead on an edge or a dot on a surface

ul: All sizes in **millimetres**, with a note to say so; do not write "mm" after every figure.
Give each size needed **once only**. If it is given twice and one is changed later, the two will not agree.
Always give the **overall** length, width and height, so the material can be cut from stock.
Place dimensions **outside** the views where possible, between projection lines.
Put **smaller dimensions nearer the view** and larger ones further out, so dimension lines and projection lines do not cross.
Do not dimension to **hidden lines** if it can be avoided: dimension the feature in the view where it is seen as a visible outline.
Never use an outline or a centre line as a dimension line.
Do not give a size that can be worked out from others in the same chain (leave one size out, or mark it as a reference).
Where parts must line up, dimension from a **datum** (a face, an edge or a centre line).

head: Method
How it works
When to use it
rows: Each size runs from the end of the one before
Where small errors adding up do not matter
Every size is measured from the same datum
Hole positions and features that must line up with other parts; errors do not add up

head: Feature
How it is dimensioned
rows: Ø before the size (Ø25), usually on the view where the part looks like a circle, or on the side view of a round part
R before the size (R10), with the dimension line drawn from the centre and the arrow touching the arc
Number, × and diameter: 4 × Ø10. Add THRU or a depth if it matters. Locate the hole centres from datums
6 × Ø14 EQ SP ON 120 PCD, with the pitch circle drawn as a thin chain line
In degrees, with the dimension line drawn as an arc

blocks.p: No part can be made to an exact size. A **tolerance** says how far the size may vary. **80 ± 0.5** means the part may be anything from **79.5 mm to 80.5 mm**. A size can also be written as two limits, one above the other (80.5 above 79.5). Sizes without their own tolerance follow the general tolerance in the title block. Give close tolerances only where they are needed: they make the part harder and dearer to make.

head: Mistake
Why it is wrong
rows: If one is changed later, the two may not agree
Dimension taken to a hidden line
Hidden lines are harder to read and easy to misread
Drawn size written instead of the real size
The part would be made to the wrong size
The reader cannot tell which arrow belongs to which line
Figures written below the line, upside down or crowded
The material cannot be cut from stock without adding up
Hole positions chained from hole to hole
Errors add up and the holes may not line up

blocks.p: A **pictorial drawing** shows three faces of an object in one view, so it is easy to picture. It is ideal for showing a customer what a part will look like and for sketching an idea. It is not usually used for making the part: orthographic views are clearer for sizes.

ul: The three main edges at the nearest corner are drawn **one vertical and two at 30° to the horizontal**, using the 30°/60° set square on the T-square.

Lengths along these three axes are drawn at their **true (scaled) length**. (Strictly, this is an isometric drawing; an isometric projection shrinks the sizes a little, and is not used in the workshop.)
Lines that are vertical on the object stay vertical on the drawing; lines parallel to an axis stay parallel to it.
Hidden lines are usually left out.

flow: Draw the vertical line of the nearest corner at its true height
From its bottom, draw lines at 30° to the left and to the right
Mark the true length on one 30° line and the true width on the other
Draw verticals up from these points and complete the top with lines parallel to the 30° lines: this is the box
Cut away the box to the shape of the part, measuring only along the isometric lines
Add holes as ellipses, then line in the visible edges thick

blocks.p: An edge that does not run along one of the three axes (a **non-isometric line**), such as the sloping edge of a gusset, cannot be measured at its true length. Find its two end points by measuring along isometric lines, then join them.
A circle on any face of an isometric drawing appears as an **ellipse**. To draw one:

flow: Draw the centre lines of the hole on the face, parallel to the face's edges
Draw an isometric square (a rhombus) round the circle, with sides equal to the diameter, touching the centre lines at their midpoints
Draw lines from each of the two wide-angle (120°) corners to the midpoints of the two far sides
Where these lines cross are the centres of the two small arcs; the two wide-angle corners are the centres of the two large arcs
Draw the four arcs, each touching the rhombus at the midpoints of its sides

blocks.p: This **four-centre method** gives a neat, close copy of a true ellipse. You can also use an ellipse template, or sketch the ellipse freehand inside the rhombus, touching the middle of each side.

ul: The front face is drawn in its **true shape**, as in a front view, so circles on it stay circles.
The receding lines (going back) are drawn at an angle, usually **45°**.
Drawn at full length (cavalier oblique), the receding lines make the object look too deep. Drawn at **half length (cabinet oblique)**, it looks more natural.
Put the face with circles, curves or the most detail at the front.

head: Point
Isometric
Oblique
rows: True circles on the front face; ellipses on other faces
Parts with circles or detail on one face

ul: Sketch with a soft pencil (HB or B), using light strokes first and darkening the lines you keep.
Keep the proportions right: compare widths with heights by eye or with the pencil held at arm's length.
Isometric grid paper helps with angles; plain grid paper helps with orthographic sketches.
Write NTS (not to scale) on a sketch and add the sizes you know.

blocks.p: A **sectional view** shows an object as if it had been cut along an imaginary plane and the front piece taken away. It shows inside details, such as bores, holes and wall thicknesses, that would otherwise be a confusing mass of hidden lines, and it makes them easier to dimension.

ul: Show where the cut is made on another view with a **cutting plane line**: a thin chain line, thick at the ends and where it changes direction, with **arrows** showing the direction of viewing and **letters** such as A–A.
Label the sectional view with the same letters: SECTION A–A.
**Hatch** the surfaces that the plane cuts through with thin lines, usually at **45°**, evenly spaced (often about 3–5 mm apart; closer on small areas).
Hatch every area of the same part in the **same direction and spacing**, even where the areas are separated, for example on each side of a bore.
Hatch parts that touch in **opposite directions**, or with different spacing, so they can be told apart.
Do not hatch bolts, nuts, washers, shafts, pins, keys and rivets cut along their length, or thin ribs and webs cut along their length: draw them in outside view.
Leave out hidden lines behind the cutting plane unless they are needed.
Very thin parts, such as gaskets and sheet, may be shown solid black.

blocks.note: Only the cut surfaces are hatched. Edges and surfaces seen beyond the cut (behind it) are drawn as visible outlines without hatching.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Drawing
What it contains
rows: One part, fully dimensioned, with its material, quantity, scale and projection, so it can be made on its own
The parts fitted together; each part numbered with an **item number** in a circle (a balloon) on a leader line; a **parts list**; the main overall sizes and any assembly notes
A table, usually above the title block: item number, description, quantity, material and the drawing number or size of each part

blocks.p: On an assembly drawing of a welded part, the welds are shown with **weld symbols**: an arrow pointing to the joint, a reference line, and a symbol such as a triangle for a fillet weld, with its size. The details differ between the ISO and the American (AWS) systems; your instructor will show you the ones the Centre uses.

head: Check
Ask yourself
rows: Are the views in the right places for the projection symbol? Do they line up? Does every edge appear in every view?
Are outlines thick, hidden lines dashed, centre lines chain, dimension lines thin? Are construction lines faint or erased?
Is every size needed there, once only, as a real size? Are the overall sizes given? Are holes located from datums?
Are Ø, R, THK, PCD and hole notes correct?
Title, drawing number, scale, projection symbol, units, material, name, date and revision all filled in?
Do the sizes match the part, the sketch or the measurements?

blocks.note: Check your own drawing first, then ask someone else to check it. A fresh pair of eyes finds mistakes you will read past.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: When an issued drawing is changed, give it a new **revision letter or number** (A, B, C or 1, 2, 3).
Record each change in the **revision table**: what changed, the date and who made the change.
Issue the new revision and withdraw the old copies, so that nobody works from an out-of-date drawing.
When you work from a drawing, check that its revision matches the job card.

blocks.p: If a size, a note or a view is missing or unclear, do not guess and do not measure it off the paper. Ask your supervisor or the person who drew it, and have the drawing corrected.
Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain why drawings follow agreed rules, and what goes wrong when they do not.
I can name the types of drawing: sketch, detail, assembly, detail view and pictorial.
I can name and use the drawing equipment and choose the right pencil for each line.
I can give the sizes of A4 and A3 paper and set out a sheet with a border and title block.
I can draw and name each type of line and say what it is used for.
I can choose the front view and the number of views for a part.
I can place the views correctly in first-angle and third-angle projection and recognise both projection symbols.
I can project sizes between views, using a 45° line for depths.
I can choose a standard scale, work out drawn sizes and real sizes, and convert inches to millimetres.
I can space the views evenly on the sheet.
I can dimension a part clearly, once only, from datums where needed, using Ø, R, hole notes and tolerances.
I can draw a part in isometric, including sloping edges and holes as ellipses.
I can draw an oblique view and explain cavalier and cabinet oblique.
I can draw a sectional view with a cutting plane, labels and correct hatching.
I can draw an assembly with item numbers and a parts list.
I can compare drawing by hand with CAD.
I can check a drawing, record a revision, store drawings properly, and ask when information is missing.

terms: A drawing showing how parts fit together, with item numbers and a parts list
Computer-aided design (or drafting): drawing with a computer program
Oblique drawing with the receding lines drawn at half length
A thin chain line marking the centre of a hole or the axis of a round part
A light, thin line used to set out a drawing before it is lined in
A thin chain line, thick at the ends, with arrows and letters, showing where a section is taken
A face, edge or line that sizes are measured from
A drawing of one part with everything needed to make it
A small area drawn again at a larger scale
A thin line with arrowheads showing the extent of a size
The view arrangement with the plan below the front view and each view on the far side from where it is seen
Thin parallel lines, usually at 45°, on the cut surfaces of a section
A thin dashed line showing an edge that cannot be seen
A pictorial drawing with one vertical axis and two axes at 30° to the horizontal
A pictorial drawing with the front face in true shape and receding lines at an angle, usually 45°
Showing an object in separate, lined-up flat views
A table of the items in an assembly, with quantity and material
Pitch circle diameter: the circle through the centres of a ring of holes
A thin line that extends from a feature to a dimension line; also called an extension line
The symbol in the title block that shows first-angle or third-angle projection
A numbered or lettered change to an issued drawing
The ratio of drawing size to real size, for example 1:2
A view of an object as if cut by a plane, showing the inside
A quick freehand drawing made without instruments
The view arrangement with the plan above the front view and each view on the side it is seen from
The panel holding the title, drawing number, scale, projection, material and names
How far a size may vary from the size given, for example ± 0.5

c1.title: A solar panel mounting plate in Falmouth
c1.text: Tajay works for a firm in Falmouth, Trelawny, that fits solar panels on roofs. He must produce a detail drawing of a steel mounting plate 500 mm long, 300 mm wide and 8 mm thick, with a 20 mm wide slot 120 mm long and four Ø14 holes that must line up with holes in the roof rails. The drawing goes on an A3 sheet, where the space inside the border is about 400 mm × 277 mm, in first-angle projection.

c2.title: Shelf brackets for a guest house in Port Antonio
c2.text: Monique runs a small welding shop in Port Antonio, Portland. A guest house owner wants steel shelf brackets, and Monique will draw one in isometric so that the owner can see what it will look like. Each bracket is an L of 6 mm plate, 60 mm wide. The upright leg is 200 mm high with a Ø10 fixing hole, the shelf leg is 150 mm long, and a triangular gusset joins the two legs.

c3.title: A pump frame drawing from overseas
c3.text: Odane works in the maintenance shop of a food factory in Kingston. A new pump has arrived from the United States with a drawing of its steel base frame. On that drawing the plan is above the front view, there is a view to the right of the front view, and the sizes are in inches. Odane must redraw one bracket from it in millimetres, in first-angle projection, for the factory's records.

c4.title: A bearing housing section near Frome
c4.text: Shelly-Ann is a trainee in the maintenance workshop of a sugar factory near Frome, Westmoreland. She must draw a sectional front view of a cast-iron bearing housing with a bronze bush pressed into its bore. Two bolts hold the housing to a steel base. The cutting plane, marked A–A on the plan, passes through the centre of the bore and through both bolts.

c5.title: Checking a classmate's drawing in St Ann's Bay
c5.text: At a training centre in St Ann's Bay, Jodian has drawn a base plate with an upright and a gusset at a scale of 1:2, and asks Romario to check it before she hands it in. Romario notices four things: the title block shows the first-angle symbol, but the plan is drawn above the front view; the 90 mm gusset edge is dimensioned 45; a 40 mm dimension is placed outside a 160 mm one, so their lines cross; and the holes have no centre lines.

questions.q: Which scale should Tajay use for the plate on the A3 sheet?
o: 1:1, so that sizes can be checked with a rule
1:10, so that there is plenty of space round it
1:2, the largest standard scale that fits well
2:1, so that the holes and slot show clearly
questions.why: At 1:1 the 500 mm plate will not fit in a 400 mm space. At 1:2 it is drawn 250 × 150 mm, leaving room for dimensions and a thickness note; 1:10 would make it needlessly small.

questions.q: The four holes must line up with holes in the roof rails. How should Tajay dimension their positions?
o: Chain each hole from the one before it, across the plate
Measure every hole position from the same datum edges
Give only the overall plate size and let the fabricator space them
Give each hole position twice, so that it cannot be missed
questions.why: Datum dimensioning stops small errors adding up from hole to hole, so the holes line up with the rails. A size given twice can end up with two values if the drawing is changed.

questions.q: After the drawing has been issued, the customer asks for the slot to be 140 mm long instead of 120 mm. What should Tajay do?
o: Cross out 120 on the issued copies and write 140 beside it
Tell the fabricator by phone and leave the drawing as it is
Draw a new sheet with the same drawing number and no note
Change it, raise the revision, record it and reissue
questions.why: A changed drawing gets a new revision letter or number, with the change, date and name in the revision table. The new revision is issued and old copies withdrawn, so nobody works to the out-of-date size.

questions.q: How should Monique draw the Ø10 hole on the face of the upright leg?
o: As a true 10 mm circle, drawn with the compass
As an ellipse inside a 10 mm isometric square
As a small square, since curves are not used
As a level ellipse 10 mm long and 5 mm high
questions.why: Circles on isometric faces appear as ellipses. Drawing a rhombus (isometric square) with sides equal to the diameter, then fitting the ellipse to touch the middle of each side, gives the right size and slant.

questions.q: The gusset's sloping edge does not run along any isometric axis. How should Monique draw it?
o: Measure its true length and draw it at 30° from the corner
Draw it at 45° with the set square, as in an oblique drawing
Leave it out, since sloping edges are not shown in isometric
Mark its end points along isometric lines, then join them
questions.why: Only lines parallel to the three isometric axes can be measured at true length. A sloping (non-isometric) edge is found by locating its ends with measurements along the axes and joining them.

questions.q: Monique also tries an oblique drawing, with the receding lines drawn full length at 45°. The bracket looks far too deep. What can she change?
o: Draw the receding lines at half their true length
Draw the receding lines at 30° instead of 45°
Draw the front face at half its true size as well
Leave out the receding lines and show only the front
questions.why: Full-length receding lines (cavalier oblique) make objects look too deep. Drawing them at half length (cabinet oblique) gives a more natural look, while the front face stays in its true shape.

questions.q: Which lines does Monique normally leave out of the finished isometric drawing?
o: The visible edges at the back of the bracket
The lines of the hole's ellipse on the upright
The thick lines along the nearest corner
The hidden edges, which would be dashed lines
questions.why: Pictorial drawings show what can be seen, so hidden (dashed) lines are usually left out, and construction lines are made faint or rubbed out. All visible edges, including the ellipse, are lined in.

questions.q: On the supplier's third-angle drawing, which side of the frame does the view placed to the right of the front view show?
o: The right-hand side, seen looking from the right
The left-hand side, seen looking from the left
The underside, seen looking up from underneath
The back of the frame, seen looking from behind it
questions.why: In third-angle projection each view is placed on the side it is seen from, so a view on the right of the front view shows the right-hand side. The plan above the front view confirms it is third angle.

questions.q: In Odane's first-angle redraw, where should the view of the right-hand side go?
o: To the right of the front view
To the left of the front view
Above the front view, over the plan
Below the plan, under the front view
questions.why: In first-angle projection each view goes on the far side of the front view from where it is seen. The view from the right therefore goes on the left, and the plan goes below the front view.

questions.q: A hole on the supplier's drawing is marked Ø0.50 in. What should Odane write on his millimetre drawing?
questions.why: 1 inch = 25.4 mm, so 0.50 in = 0.5 × 25.4 = 12.7 mm. He should check with his supervisor whether the hole must suit an inch bolt before rounding it.

questions.q: Which description matches the first-angle symbol that Odane must draw in his title block?
o: A cone's side view, with its end view of two circles beside the small end
A cone's side view, with its end view of two circles beside the large end
A cube drawn in isometric, with an arrow showing the viewing direction
A circle with the letters 1ST inside it, drawn next to the scale
questions.why: Both symbols show a cone with its top cut off as a trapezium and two circles. In first angle the circles sit beside the large end of the trapezium; in third angle, beside the small end.

questions.q: How should the two bolts be shown in Section A–A?
o: Hatched at 45°, in the same way as the housing
Drawn in outside view, with no hatching
Left out of the section altogether
Filled in solid black so that they stand out
questions.why: Bolts, nuts, shafts and pins cut along their length are not hatched; they are drawn as if uncut, which makes the drawing easier to read. Only the housing and the bush are hatched.

questions.q: How should Shelly-Ann label the sectional view?
o: FRONT ELEVATION, since it takes the front view's place
VIEW B, the letter after the one on the plan
SECTION A–A, the letters on the cutting plane
CUT VIEW, so the reader knows it has been cut
questions.why: The sectional view carries the same letters as the cutting plane line on the plan, so the reader can match the view to the place where the cut was made and the direction of the arrows.

questions.q: The housing's cut surface shows as two separate areas, one on each side of the bore. How should they be hatched?
o: In opposite directions, to show that they are separate
One area hatched and the other left plain to save time
With closer spacing on the area nearer to the bolts
The same direction and spacing, as they are one part
questions.why: Every area of one part is hatched the same way, so the reader can see they belong together. The bronze bush, a different part touching the housing, is hatched in the opposite direction or with different spacing.

questions.q: What should Romario tell Jodian about the position of her plan?
o: In first angle the plan belongs below the front view
The plan may go above or below, as long as it lines up
The plan should be drawn on its own on a second sheet
The plan should be placed to the right of the front view
questions.why: The views must match the projection symbol. With the first-angle symbol, a plan above the front view will be misread, so she moves it below (or, if she meant third angle, changes the symbol).

questions.q: The gusset edge is 90 mm long on the real part. What should its dimension say on Jodian's 1:2 drawing?
o: 45, the length measured on her drawing
90, the real length of the gusset edge
45 (1:2), with the scale written beside it
180, twice the length measured on paper
questions.why: Dimensions always give the real size, whatever the scale, because the part is made to the numbers written. The scale only sets how big the drawing is.

questions.q: How should the 40 mm and the 160 mm dimensions be arranged so that their lines do not cross?
o: The 160 mm one nearer the view, the 40 mm one outside it
Both on the same dimension line, one written over the other
The 40 mm one nearer the view, the 160 mm one further out
The 40 mm one written inside the outline of the view
questions.why: Smaller dimensions go nearer the view and larger ones further out, so projection lines and dimension lines do not cross. Dimensions are kept outside the views where possible.

questions.q: How should the centre lines of the holes be drawn?
o: Thin chain lines crossing at the hole centre and running a little past each hole
Thick continuous lines crossing at the centre of each hole and stopping at its edge
Thin dashed lines running right across the whole view through every hole
Short freehand ticks on the edge of each hole at the top and at the side
questions.why: Centre lines are thin chain lines that cross at long dashes at the centre and run a few millimetres past the feature. Dashed lines mean hidden edges, and thick lines mean visible outlines.

questions.q: A shop in Bull Bay makes the same steel gate in five widths. What is the main time-saving if it uses CAD for the drawings?
o: The program decides by itself which views the gate needs
No dimensions are needed, as the printer scales the gate
The drawing never needs to be checked by anyone
One drawing can be copied and changed for each width
questions.why: CAD lets a drawing be copied, edited and reprinted quickly, so five widths need one careful drawing and four quick changes. The drawings still need the right views, full dimensions and checking.

questions.q: An A4 sheet is 210 mm × 297 mm. What size is an A3 sheet?
questions.why: Each A size is double the one below it: two A4 sheets side by side along their long edges make A3, 297 × 420 mm. 420 × 594 mm is A2.
